secondBeat: They hold no number at all.
mechanism: The longer start, middle and end guard bars encode no digit; they mark the label, split the digits and set the timing for the scanner
expectedConsequence: A scanner can detect the label and tell which half it is reading
misconception: Every stripe looks like data, but the longest bars carry no digit.
payoff: The longest bars are signposts for the scanner, not data.

narration.text: Some barcode bars are longer, and that's deliberate.
They hold no number at all.
On a UPC barcode, the start, middle and end guard bars extend lower.
They encode no digit; they split the code into two halves.
IBM's George Laurer was assigned to design a supermarket scanner label.
His team defined guard bars so a scanner could detect the label.
They even told it which half it was reading.
So the longest bars are signposts, not data.

researchEvidence.claim: The start, middle and end guard bars of a UPC-A barcode extend further down than the digit bars.
Guard patterns do not encode a digit; they help decoding.
The guard patterns separate the two groups of six digits and establish the timing.
A UPC-A barcode has exactly 30 bars: 6 form guard patterns and 24 represent its 12 digits.
IBM assigned George Laurer to determine how to make a supermarket scanner and label.
Laurer and a colleague defined guard bars and how a scanner should detect the label.
The guard bars also identified which half of the label was being read and trained the scanner's threshold circuits.
Splitting the label into two halves allowed the bars to be cut nearly in half in length.
The first UPC-marked item scanned at a retail checkout was Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum in Troy, Ohio, on 26 June 1974.
